articles.title: A new Go API for JSON
articles.content: Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil 4 November 2026 Introduction JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago! Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes. After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment , describing the problems with encoding/json , and an introduction to the new packages. Problems with encoding/json Overall, encoding/json has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings. Behavior flaws There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json : Imprecise handling of JSON syntax : Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value. encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream. encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635 ). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names. Leaking nilness of slices and maps : JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null , this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty J
articles.summary: Go 团队发布全新 JSON API，由多位核心开发者设计，旨在提升 Go 语言 JSON 编解码的性能与易用性。

articles.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
articles.content: Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds. As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history. AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year. Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%. (Image credit: AMD) The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft , OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems. AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025. "We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth." Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter. (Image credit: AMD) Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 bill

articles.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
articles.content: In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability , which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA , Wikipedia , the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server. As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI. “One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche , AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo . “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.” PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed. “If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana , an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University . “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI . Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately. Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity
articles.summary: PHP2Shell 等重大漏洞暴露了数十年的技术债，AI 的普及正迫使行业加速偿还这些历史遗留问题。

articles.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
articles.content: Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model. To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains. Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview , a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4). Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face , Together AI , GMI Cloud , and OpenRouter . Fireworks goes live later today.
articles.summary: Ricursive Intelligence 发布 Ripple-65B 预览版，在美国开源权重模型中创下智能体编程新纪录。

articles.title: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS
articles.content: It was just a boring Saturday afternoon, and I thought I'd fix some of the problems with my homelab. One of those problems was that an external site my Podman container was trying to talk to just wasn't working. I kept getting "Site cannot be reached" almost immediately. This made me suspect something was wrong with my DNS setup, so I started doing a dig on the domain. I tried different providers, Google DNS, Cloudflare, pretty much everyone. Almost all of them returned the same IP address. But as soon as I tried Cloudflare's DoH endpoint, I got a completely different IP address. "Huh?" was my exact reaction. I took the IP I got from the first DNS resolution and tried to look up who owned it. Lo and behold, it was my goddamn ISP. That's when I realised my ISP was hijacking my DNS queries and returning a tampered IP address. Well, the obvious answer was DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoH (DNS over HTTPS). I made a tweet about this, and it somehow blew up . But going through the replies, I noticed quite a few misconceptions and questions that I couldn't answer one by one. So I figured I'd use this article to address some of those questions and clear up a few misconceptions along the way. I self host Unbound I am safe For those of you who don't know, Unbound is basically a DNS resolver, kind of like what Cloudflare runs at 1.1.1.1 . The difference is, you can run it locally. It works by querying DNS servers to figure out the IP address for a domain, starting at the root nameservers and eventually making its way to the domain's authoritative nameserver. Now here's the catch. DNS resolution doesn't happen over a single connection. Your resolver might have to talk to multiple nameservers to figure out an IP address, and these queries are traditionally sent over plaintext DNS, usually UDP. Which means, you guessed it, your ISP can snoop on or even tamper with your DNS traffic. But you can also configure a forward-zone in Unbound. Instead of resolving DNS queries itself, Unbound can forward them to another DNS resolver. And if that resolver supports DoT, the connection to it is encrypted, which means your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS queries in transit. Just use DNSSEC It's understandable why someone would assume DNSSEC is what protects them here. I mean, it has DNS and Security right in the name. And in a way, it does, but it works through verification, not encryption. You see, DNSSEC doesn't encrypt your DNS traffic before sending it to a resolver. It uses cryptographic signatures to verify that the DNS data is authentic and hasn't been tampered with. But the problem here remains the same: your DNS traffic is still unencrypted in transit. Which means, your ISP can still snoop on it or mess with the responses. And for DNSSEC validation to work, the domain you're querying needs to have DNSSEC properly configured, with valid signatures and a chain of trust. And here's another problem: according to the October 2026 Defaults.Exposed census , o
articles.summary: 作者发现自家 ISP 在劫持 DNS 请求，排查后揭示了运营商层面的流量劫持行为及其影响。

articles.title: Shlemiel the Painter Is Back: How Zig’s libc Rewrite Made SQLite Slower
articles.content: Spolsky Wisdom Back in 2001, Joel Spolsky – whose writings had a big influence my career – wrote a great piece titled Back to Basics . The premise of the piece is that practitioners should understand the basics: However abstract and remote we may seem from the basic algorithms that drive computing, they can unexpectedly have enormous consequences on our projects. One of his examples is the “Shlemiel the Painter” trap, where a seemingly simple choice leads to quadratic runtime complexity. In that parable, a street line painter never moves his can of paint. As he gets further and further along in the line, increasingly more of his time is spent walking to and from his can of paint. It is astonishing how often this Shlemiel the Painter pattern recurs 1 , including now in 2026. My Chess Analysis Service Staggers Under Load A few days ago I posted about a chess analysis service I put online ↗ 2 . This is primarily a Rust service backed by sqlite that dishes out analysis tasks to runners. Each runner processes upwards of hundreds of chess games and return a large set of JSON bundles back to the main service, where they are processed and then stuffed into sqlite. While the analysis pegs two dozen cores on a runner for minutes on end, the process of storing the data should take milliseconds. Sub-milliseconds. Imagine my surprise when on the first really large set of games, the simple process of inserting the JSON data – maybe about 40,000 records – into the data store took minutes . During all of my testing this never really appeared as a critical path, but with a large set of records it suddenly was a breaking problem. What made this more perplexing was that it completely saturated a core, being a CPU-bound operation. How could inserting simple JSON into SQLite yield minutes of CPU time? Shlemiel the painter has made an appearance. To drop a spoiler, he was introduced to the project via Zig’s cc compiler and its replacement for standard library functions. A Minor Issue In Zig Becomes A Major Performance Issue The project isn’t built in Zig, but instead uses Rust. The sqlx sqlite crate needs to be compiled for the target environment – sqlite is of course a C project – so to facilitate cross-platform building, generating both Mac ARM64 and Linux ARM64 / x86-64 binaries from this machine in a convenient build and deploy workflow, zig cc is used to compile sqlite when targeting Linux, generously offering up cross-platform targeting via cargo-zigbuild. From one build and deploy script on my Mac I can target all of my platforms without containers or build machines. Zig’s elegant libzigc re-implements the standard library so you can static link the necessary functionality. Zig uses musl (the standard library rewrite), but they have been rewriting it piece by piece in pure Zig (via libzigc), removing the C dependencies one at a time. And that’s where the performance issue was introduced. In the rewrite of strspn , replacing the musl version with the pure zig va
articles.summary: Zig 重写 libc 后导致 SQLite 性能下降，文章借用 Shlemiel 画家的比喻分析性能退化原因。

articles.title: Your Cryptography Conspiracy Theory Is Wrong
articles.content: This conversation plays out hundreds of times a day, but (thankfully) only a handful of those involve me: Person: “I have [problem].” Cryptography nerd: “Oh, you probably want to use [sensible recommendation].” Person: “Ah, well, can I really trust that? The NSA probably backdoored it 30 years ago. Dual_EC, amirite?!” Cryptography nerd: … Koblitz and Menezes, unheard: “ You fucking wot m8? “ Conspiracy theories about the NSA and/or NIST are a dime a dozen these days. And, ever since the Snowden disclosures in 2013, I am politically primed to directionally agree with distrusting the US government wholesale. But most of the technical arguments baked into folks’ conspiracy theories make no goddamn sense . This distrust is not exclusive to only the US government. The goal of this blog post is not to convince you that you should trust any government; just that they are not magical or omniscient. To that end, I’m going to explore some of the history of NSA, NIST, and cryptography standardization. Then, to explore some of the conspiracy theories that were being floated about such activity, and what we’ve learned in the years since (especially in the past month). Finally, I’m going to examine some of the current conspiracy theories floating around message boards and social media today, and explain why they’re almost certainly wrong. Buckle up, this is going to be a tedious one. Why should we listen to you? If you find yourself asking a question like this, the correct answer is simply, “You shouldn’t.” After all, I have never held (let alone even applied for) a security clearance, and have no access to any non-public information. I’m also not a current or former government employee, and have no aspirations to ever become one. I have access to all the same facts anyone else does. In balance, I have no horse in the race of who trusts whom. I’m just tired of hearing the same poorly reasoned arguments all the damn time, and would like to stop having to repeat myself when I encounter one. Historical NSA Shenanigans The sources for this, by the way, are the declassified United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and United States Cryptologic History . DES VIDEO No, not that DES. The Data Encryption Standard (DES) was published in the Federal Register in 1975 and then standardized in 1977. We consider it weak these days, but DES was a real game-changer for its time: It offered a standard block cipher to use for sensitive (but not classified) commercial applications. Prior to DES, the history of cryptography was largely about military uses (except a few quirky mathematicians here and there), going back before Caesar’s cipher . From declassified documents, we now know the full story, but from the time that DES was first standardized, up until recent years, there have been a concerns about NSA’s involvement . We sent the S-boxes off to Washington. They came back and were all different. Alan Konheim, quoted in Applied Cryptography , p. 280 To say that aca

articles.title: Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode
articles.content: We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark. In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright . Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web. You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’. For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark. How does Adaptive Dark Mode work? At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged. While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio . Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark. Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear. It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos. Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict. It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformatio
articles.summary: Safari 27.3 beta 推出自适应深色模式，可自动将浅色网站转为深色显示，提升夜间浏览体验。

articles.title: C++26 Disapproved
articles.content: On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved ! I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views. The Current Status As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote. In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures , there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved. The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release. The Process Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree. However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently. The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026. It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me. The History of Contracts in C++ The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was remov

articles.title: How to speed up the Rust compiler in November 2026
articles.content: My first month working on Rust compiler performance for Hexcat is over and it’s time to see some of what’s happened since my last post . Spans Spans are a critical data structure in the Rust compiler. Every AST, HIR, and MIR node carries a span. Each span has four fields recording the following. A source location ( lo and hi ). A crate’s source files are concatenated into a single buffer, and these are indices into that buffer. Possibly some hygiene and provenance data ( context ), relevant for macros and other things. Possibly an extra relative position ( parent ) that is used to minimize the compile time impact of small changes to source locations, such as those caused by inserting a single line at the start of a file. Each of the four fields is 32 bits, resulting in 16 bytes of data. But most of the time these 16 bytes can be compressed into one of three 8-byte inline formats, and the remaining cases are interned into a global table. This works by taking advantage of patterns in the data: many source locations have a small length (i.e. a small difference between lo and hi ); many spans have a zero context and/or parent, and the non-zero contexts and parents are typically small integers; parents are only used in incremental builds. #163857 : In this PR I replace the old compression scheme with one that is simpler and more efficient. For incremental builds we now typically intern around 1% of spans compared to 20-40% with the old scheme. (In non-incremental builds we typically intern fewer than 0.1%.) Also, we can always store the context field inline even in the interned case, which is useful because we often read the context by itself. This change reduced instruction counts across many benchmarks, in the best cases by more than 3%, and the cycle count improvements were even higher. Incremental builds saw the largest improvements due to less interning. #163971 : In this PR Josh Triplett took advantage of the new representation to micro-optimize a number of span operations. This reduced instruction counts across many benchmarks, in the best case by more than 2%. #164291 : In this PR I tried using a pattern type to give Span a niche so that Option<Span> would be the same size as Span . It worked but didn’t help performance because we don’t use Option<Span> much, and it made the code more complicated. So I abandoned it. #163628 : During metadata encoding/decoding and stable hashing we typically need to get information about the same parent span from a hash table over and over. In this PR I put a single-entry cache in front of that hash table, which avoids the hash table lookup in most cases. This reduced instruction counts on many benchmarks, in the best case by more than 4%, mostly benefiting incremental compilation. New trait solver #163981 , #164234 , #165160 : In these three PRs I focused on the compilation time of Diesel , a crate for which the in-development new trait solver is slower than the old trait solver. I did a dozen or so micro-opti

articles.title: Observations from Running stealmybitcoin.com
articles.content: Table of Contents Last week, I saw an article on the front page of the New York Times website reporting that a critical vulnerability in PHP had been found. The article, and others like it , claimed any attacker could achieve arbitrary remote code execution on any of the millions of running PHP services worldwide simply by sending a few unauthenticated web requests that exploited the PHP2Shell vulnerability. My office Slack was buzzing, as were several of my Signal chats with colleagues and friends across the security community. Rumors swirled about how in-the-wild exploitation caused one tech company to break embargo and leak news of the vulnerability hours before the rest of the community could coordinate disclosure. That hackers were already hacking websites, in the wild, with this exploit and that every hour mattered to get the patches rolled out across 70% of the internet. The Question Was PHP2Shell the hallmark of a new era whereby uplifted randos could hack any website with a few well-crafted prompts to an AI model? I looked out my window, expecting perhaps to see the dull apocalyptic glow of fires on the horizon as society collapsed in real time. Nothing. While online articles and tweets made the rounds about the eleven alarm cyberapocalypse upon us, I struggled to find any reference to a specific website that had been hacked. Over the following days, a few iconoclasts had pointed out that the vulnerability was rather fiddly in practice ( Elias Taylor ; Lucas Luitjes ) and that hacker groups, while initially quite excited by the exploit’s potential, had started to view it as impractical or difficult ( KELA ). Yet at the same time, the national and international press continued to cover a herculean emergency effort to hunt down and patch PHP-based websites across the internet. Rather than wait around and wonder, I decided to try to figure things out for myself. I had two fundamental questions: Was PHP2Shell actually exploitable outside of a lab environment? Would relatively unskilled attackers with access to AI and the PHP source code be able to exploit this class of vulnerability? The Results Directly, the answers to the questions are: 1) Was PHP2Shell actually exploitable outside of a lab environment? Yes. Absolutely. The challenge winner, who has posted a writeup , exploited my server directly over an open internet connection and did so using the PHP2Shell vulnerability (e.g. he did not exploit some other vulnerability in my setup). He did this through a specially crafted exploit which targeted the specific configuration of my PHP installation and the ways in which it was set up on the server. 2) Would relatively unskilled attackers with access to AI and the PHP source code be able to exploit this class of vulnerability? Not yet. Of tens of thousands of people who attempted the exploit - including in a 9 hour period when the challenge was active after the first successful solve (more on that below…) - only two managed to trigger the pri

articles.title: Death comes for XSLT
articles.content: Tuesday 3 Nov 2026 Last halloween, Google decided to kill XSLT . That was not a unilateral decision mind you, Google said “jump” and other browser vendors said “how high?” In response, I published my Intent to Deprecate and Remove Google Chrome . A performative declaration of course, I don’t install spyware. Fearing my parody lacked seriousness, I created XSLT.RIP to ensure the developer world was informed of Google’s death note . This did the trick, although a few commenters believed it was satire. There is subtlety to XSLT.RIP . The website itself is built with XSLT and when Google kills XSLT they’ll kill my website. The web standards process and its stewards ( Big Browser ) used to adhere to a social contract. Backwards compatibility was a major design principle. Under no circumstances do you ever purposefully break the web. Google decided to renege and break the web. XSLT.RIP will be broken soon and I’ll sit back and watch Google break it. 17 November 2026 appears to be the date of execution. Some Chromium-based browsers have been running a man-in-the-middle attack by injecting propaganda into XSLT websites. This site uses XSLT; that functionality is being removed from this browser very soon. When that happens, this page will likely no longer display correctly. You might be able to install a browser extension that allows you to continue viewing it. Otherwise, you should contact the maintainer of the site for further information. Source: This site uses XSLT: what Chrome’s banner means - XSLT Playground This appears to be an <xslt-warning-banner> custom element that fails to render when it violates content security policy . Alt Two examples of the XSLT warning banner quoted above. The first is white text on a red background, the second is broken default HTML styles. I’m testing on ungoogled-chromium so who knows how it’s intended to look. The line of death is another “social contract” that Google has forgotten. They’re blaming website owners and acting like questionable purveyors of free public Wi-Fi. This is arrogant and intrusive. “contact the maintainer of the site” — you broke the web Google, own it at least.

articles.title: vercel-labs/agent-desktop (Rust)
articles.content: Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree. agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library. Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads. npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64. For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable. On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: brew install agent-desktop . There is no official Scoop package yet. The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket. Release archives and building from source are covered in Installation . agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot: { "version" : " 2.6 " , "ok" : true , "command" : " snapshot " , "data" : { "app" : " Finder " , "snapshot_id" : " s8f3k2p9 " , "ref_count" : 59 , "complete" : true , "tree" : { "role" : " window " , "name" : " Downloads " , "children" : [ { "role" : " treeitem " , "name" : " Documents " , "ref_id" : " @s8f3k2p9:e8 " , "available_actions" : [ " Click " ] } ] } } } Refs carry their snapshot id. A bare @e8 fails with INVALID_ARGS . If the UI changed, an action returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET . Take a new snapshot and use its refs. Actions are headless by default: no pointer movement, no focus change. Pass --headed for physical input. type , set-value , and clipboard-set accept --stdin for piped text, keeping it out of process arguments. Run secret steps as separate commands; batch JSON text appears in process arguments. In PowerShell, quote every ref ( '@s8f3k2p9:e8' ), because a bare @token is the splatting operator. The full walkthrough is in the quick start . Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through PlatformAdapter . Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API. The binary carries guides that match its version: agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules agent-desktop skills get platform #

articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: 企业应用AI报告显示：AI发现安全漏洞的速度远超团队修复能力，部分公司AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续扩张。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中AI生成或增强的广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI标签；最大亲AI超级PAC向空壳公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备；该话题成为AI专家本周分享最多的链接。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖AI模型在自主开展AI研究的测试中失败；专家关注AI治理话语权、军事规划应用及向个人电脑渗透等议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型；大规模部署已进入日常使用，同时AI被限制或移除的场景也在增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务；剑桥因AI训练条款拒绝Turnitin，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI已深度进入校园。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta的AI电话代理被曝背后有真人接线员；自动化转人工、私密提示词被审查等隐藏环节暴露，AI代理透明度受质疑。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI实验室在未就故障报告标准达成一致前便发布代理产品；私聊被读取、模型自写记忆、插件静默更新等问题引发监管关注。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr提出“Kerr定律”，指出当前限制团队的核心是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建成果保持同步，尤其在代理写代码时代。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres生态扩张：核心刻意保持简单，扩展生态繁荣，pg_lake引入DuckDB与Iceberg，并讨论AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 分享如何将邮件服务扩展至300万用户，揭秘背后的Go重写与面向AI代理的构建思路。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen 讲述周末40小时项目 NanoClaw 如何成为爆款开源项目，并发展为专注容器隔离安全的企业AI公司。

On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 讨论开源仓库可能已被攻陷的猜想，以及AI如何降低开发门槛。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale CEO Sam Lambert 介绍5美元Postgres、Vitess重写、AI代理提交schema变更及500TB表秒级回滚。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 蜜罐与数字绊线，用于检测攻击者触碰AWS密钥等入侵行为。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber 回顾 react-boilerplate 等开源项目历程，现于 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录与应用平台。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 讲解 Code Mode 如何让单个 MCP 服务器以约1000 token 暴露2500个API端点。

articles.title: Axon Sued Over AI-Powered License Plate Reader Network
articles.content: Axon has been sued in a proposed class action accusing the Taser and police body-camera maker of illegally collecting and storing license plate data on millions of California drivers through its AI-powered surveillance network. Reuters reports the details: - The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Tuesday in federal court in San Francisco by law firms Hausfeld and Gibbs Mura, alleges Axon has failed to comply with a California privacy provision by not disclosing how it collects, uses and shares plate data gathered through its camera systems - "Axon has created a mass-surveillance infrastructure that is practically impossible to avoid," the lawsuit said - Scottsdale, Arizona-based Axon did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit said the company has more than 1,000 cameras in California and alleges millions of drivers may have been affected - Some Axon cameras are installed in high-traffic areas and collect plate information as vehicles pass by. Other cameras are placed inside police vehicles, the lawsuit said - The proposed class covers drivers whose vehicle plate information was captured by an automated license plate reader in California and processed or stored by Axon's system since 2023 - The lawsuit seeks more than $5 million in damages, in addition to a court order stopping Axon from its allegedly unlawful practices Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Axon 因AI车牌识别网络非法收集存储数百万加州司机数据，在加州面临集体诉讼。

articles.title: OpenAI Says ChatGPT Is Catching Up to Google In Search
articles.content: Adam Fry, OpenAI's consumer product lead for ChatGPT, says the number of searches performed through ChatGPT has grown to roughly 20% of Google's search volume. The company defines a search as a ChatGPT query that triggers a web search, suggesting the chatbot is becoming an increasingly significant competitor to traditional search engines. The Verge reports: Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google's 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it -- now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.) As for ads, which OpenAI started testing earlier this year, Fry said they haven't produced a lasting backlash. "Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product," he said, adding that "most people do not seem to mind ads in the product." Last month, OpenAI announced plans to introduce images of sponsored products and services in ChatGPT. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: OpenAI 称 ChatGPT 搜索量已达谷歌约20%，聊天机器人正成为重要的搜索入口。

articles.title: Netflix Launches First AI-Branded Content Recommendations Feature on TVs
articles.content: Netflix is testing its first consumer-facing feature explicitly branded as AI-powered. Called "AI Discover," the feature generates personalized TV and movie recommendations in real time based on viewing history, preferences, trending content and selectable themes like "Something Light" or "Quick Watches." Variety reports: The streamer will begin rolling out AI Discover in the U.S. to customers who use Netflix in English on supported smart TVs. If you have access to it, you will see a "Discover" tab with a red gem-shaped icon and a "New" label in the top navigation bar on your TV. The company plans to expand the feature to more regions and customers in the coming weeks. Netflix has long used machine-learning and AI technologies to personalize content recommendations, but AI Discover is the first user-facing application that the company is branding as powered by artificial intelligence. The hope is that the AI-recommended titles will be another tool to drive up Netflix's total watch time among viewers, especially in the U.S. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Netflix 在电视端测试首个明确标注AI的推荐功能 AI Discover，基于观看历史实时生成个性化推荐。

articles.title: Waymo Cuts Ties With Uber, Will Serve Riders Directly
articles.content: Waymo plans to end its exclusive Uber robotaxi partnership in Austin and Atlanta in January 2028 and let customers hail its vehicles directly through the Waymo app. In an interview on The Circuit, Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana called the current Uber experience a "crapshoot" because riders aren't guaranteed a Waymo. Bloomberg reports: "In the early days, we would partner because we didn't have the scale, and in that partnering, it was a little bit of a crapshoot. Will I get a Waymo? Will I not get a Waymo?," Mawakana said in a wide-ranging interview on The Circuit with Emily Chang. She cited customers' growing demand for a consistent offering from a single app, especially from riders from San Francisco or other markets, where Waymo offers the self-driving service via its own consumer app that competes with Uber. "It's important for us to have that relationship with the rider. We've gotten that feedback from the riders in those markets," Mawakana said. "And at the same time, learning and partnering with Uber has been a really important part of our journey," she added. [...] The comments reflect Waymo's evolving relationship with the ride-hailing giant as the Alphabet unit trials different pathways to commercialize its capital-intensive autonomous technology. Waymo has leaned on partners like Uber and Lyft, as well as fleet management companies, to help operate its roughly 4,000 vehicles across the US. The company currently does more than 500,000 trips per week in 14 cities. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Waymo 将于2028年1月终止与 Uber 在奥斯汀和亚特兰大的独家合作，改为通过自家应用直接接单。

articles.title: French Blood Banks Hit Alongside Cyberattack On European Supermarkets
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: The refrigerators at three regional blood banks in France were hit by a cyberattack overnight between Sunday and Monday, at the same time hackers struck supermarkets from Sweden to Belgium. "Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems," the health ministry said in a statement. The incident had no impact on blood supplies, EFS spokesperson Charley Dubois said. "We have staff round the clock since blood can be needed at any time. They were warned about the problems by alerts and moved the blood to other refrigerators that were not connected," she said. [...] Investigations are under way into how the attack was carried out, what equipment may have been affected and when systems can safely return to service. The attack followed a similar incident in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 法国三家地区血库冰箱与瑞典至比利时的超市同期遭黑客攻击，引发对关键基础设施安全的担忧。

articles.title: Japanese Bank to Stop Allowing ATM Cards, PCs For Account Access
articles.content: Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group plans to launch Emut Bank in early 2027 as the first digital bank affiliated with a major Japanese financial institution to eliminate ATM cards, "instead having customers confirm identities using the bank's smartphone app for additional security amid a rising tide of cyberattacks," reports Nikkei Asia Review. The smartphone app will also be the only way to manage deposits, with no PC-based banking. From the report: Security has become a greater concern recently. As artificial intelligence advances, Japan has seen a surge in cyberattacks targeting companies, as well as a rise in phishing attacks aimed at stealing personal information, often targeting bank accounts. The technology being used by Emut was developed by Seven Bank, the consumer finance unit of Seven & i Holdings, operator of 7-Eleven convenience stores. Emut customers will be able to withdraw money from Seven Bank's roughly 28,000 ATMs. The network is expected to gradually expand to cover the 16,000 or so ATMs at FamilyMart convenience stores. Although MUFG Bank ATMs will not be accessible, MUFG will consider changing this in the future. Scrapping cash cards represents a shift in what has for decades been consumers' main method of withdrawing money. The former Sumitomo Bank -- a predecessor of Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. -- is believed to have been Japan's first bank to implement cash cards, in 1969. The step away from cash cards by MUFG, Japan's largest financial institution, is likely to spur other banks to follow suit. [...] Eschewing cash cards will reduce Emut's costs, which will let it offer interest rates on deposits that are expected to be higher than MUFG Bank's usual 0.5%, depending on the terms. Interest can be paid out daily, rather than twice a year -- a first for a Japanese bank. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 三菱日联金融集团计划2027年初推出数字银行 Emut Bank，取消ATM卡与电脑访问，仅用手机应用验证身份。

articles.title: Canva To Cut Or Relocate 22% of Global Workforce
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Canva is cutting or relocating more than 1,200 jobs, representing 22% of its global workforce, as part of a major restructure that includes laying off staff who helped build the Australian-founded design platform. The changes mirror a trend across the technology sector, where software companies are fighting to stay competitive against cheaper artificial intelligence disrupters while aggressively embedding AI tools themselves. [...] The restructure will affect 1,271 people, according to the company, as it focuses on "collapsing layers" and bringing "more teams together in person." [...] Those leaving Canva will receive at least six months of salary and retain healthcare coverage for a further 12 months in countries where workers receive that benefit. They can also keep their laptops. Those leaving can also apply for US$10,000 (A$14,000) grants to start their own ventures. Canva's chief executive, Melanie Perkins, said the restructure was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history." "For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralized hubs," she said. "Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Canva 宣布裁员或迁移逾1200个岗位，占全球员工22%，作为重大重组的一部分。

articles.title: NASA's Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth
articles.content: joshuark shares a report from Wired: After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft -- which is roughly as big as a large elevator -- will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low. The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about the evolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and the destruction of stars by black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth's atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without a propulsion system capable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered. The U.S. Space Force now expects Swift to reenter Earth's atmosphere around November 6. Most of the spacecraft is expected to burn up, although some components could survive and reach the ground (but most likely the ocean). "The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors," Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components, told Space.com. "Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down -- nothing recognizable as a telescope." "NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published," Sladen said regarding the risk assessment. "Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork." Read more of this story at S
articles.summary: NASA 的 Swift 天文台在轨22年、今夏救援失败后，预计下周坠落地球，落点未知。

articles.title: We Migrated 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in 3 Weeks: The Honest, AI-Assisted Truth
articles.content: A note on the Vitest version: This migration was carried out in August 2026, using Vitest 4 . All the figures, benchmarks, configuration details, and lessons described in this article refer to Vitest 4, not Vitest 5. Migrating a test runner is rarely a magic "swap and go" operation. Our experience moving our entire frontend test suite from Jest to Vitest was a real engineering undertaking, filled with bottlenecks, meticulous pool tuning, unmasked bugs, one rollback, and one optimization we shipped and then had to take back. Over the course of about three weeks, our frontend team migrated eight repositories. We didn't settle for file counts; we ran every suite end-to-end to get the real numbers. Here is the exact scale of what we achieved: 10,144 executed unit tests, real numbers from actually running the suites, not file counts. 1,799 test files across 8 repositories. 0 repos left in a half-migrated state. ~3 weeks to complete the entire effort, migrations plus the tuning that followed. ~$751 estimated AI token cost for the Claude Code sessions we could trace to this work. See the caveats on that number below: it's a rough upper bound, not a bill. This is the story of what actually happened, drawn directly from our git history, PR bodies, and session logs, to help you navigate your own migration. To save you some of the pain we went through, we also published a generalized version of the AI automation skill we ended up wishing we'd had from day one: github.com/Subito-it/articles-code/tree/main/jest-to-vitest-migration . Why Jest started hurting We didn't decide to migrate just because "Jest is slow" in the abstract. We migrated because maintaining it had become an active, recurring tax on our engineering time. We also wanted to be on the side of where the ecosystem was heading, since Vitest was fast becoming the default choice for new Vite/Next.js projects. 1. The CommonJS vs. ESM nightmare By default, next/jest skips transforming anything inside node_modules , so when a dependency ships an ESM-only update, Jest's CommonJS require() fails. We found ourselves hand-patching transformIgnorePatterns regexes to allow-list specific packages. Here's the exact code comment from our config, verbatim: // ESM-only node_modules that Jest must transform. next/jest overwrites any // user-supplied transformIgnorePatterns to skip all of node_modules, so we // allow-list these on the resolved config instead. const esmPackagesToTransform = [ ' cookie ' ]; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Separately, and about six weeks before we'd even decided to migrate: a major version bump of uuid shipped as pure ESM and broke Jest outright. The real commit message: "uuid v14 ships as pure ESM which breaks Jest (CommonJS). Replace the single usage of uuid() ... with the native crypto.randomUUID() ... removing the dependency entirely." Rather than fight the transform config again, the team just deleted the dependency. When your test runner is dictating your dependency

articles.title: Repo-Atlas - Any GitHub user’s work, mapped and clustered, with stale favorites flagged.
articles.content: Type a GitHub username, get the map of what they've actually built: repos clustered by topic, the highlight of each group, and stars over time. Live: https://evoluteur.github.io/repo-atlas/ · permalink per user: ?u=<username> The map. Every public repo as a disc (area ∝ stars), grouped into regions of repos that share topics. Hover for details, click to open the repo. Groups by stars. The legend ranks the regions by the stars they hold, so you see where the attention actually sits. Highlights. The most-starred repo in each group as a card, with its description, language and live-demo link. Hover a card to find its group on the map; the share card lists the top three. Stars over time. Without a token: stars held today, stacked by the year each repo was born. With a token: real cumulative star history per group, from stargazer dates. Share. A 1200×630 card for social posts and a permalink. Each repo's topics are normalised (plurals folded, generic tags like javascript , svg , ui dropped) and hyphenated topics also contribute their parts ( sacred-geometry → sacred , geometry ). Tokens are weighted by inverse document frequency across the account. Tokens used once, or by more than 45% of repos, carry no signal and are dropped. Repos with almost no topics fall back to description words. Repos are compared by cosine similarity and merged bottom-up (average linkage) until no two groups are more than 0.16 alike. The eight groups holding the most stars get a color and a two-word name (the tokens most frequent inside the group and rarest outside it). Everything else folds into loners . All of this is in src/atlas.js : pure functions, no DOM, tested with node --test . Everything runs in the browser against the public GitHub REST API. The map and the highlights work anonymously (60 requests/hour per IP; a typical account takes 2). GitHub only lists when each star was given to authenticated callers, so the star-history chart needs a token. A fine-grained token with no extra permissions is enough. It is kept in sessionStorage for the tab and only sent to api.github.com . Big repos are sampled: every stargazer page for repos under 500 stars, otherwise the first, last and three evenly spaced pages. Each fetched star is an exact (count, date) point; months in between are interpolated. Results are cached in localStorage (repos 1 hour, star history 24 hours). If the API can't be reached (rate limit, offline), the page lets you paste the JSON from api.github.com/users/<login>/repos?per_page=100 and maps that instead. No build step. Serve the folder and open it: npx serve . # or: python3 -m http.server open http://localhost:3000/ ? u=evoluteur npm test # clustering, highlights and timeline math npm run build # dist/repo-atlas.html: one self-contained file index.html page shell src/atlas.js clustering, highlights, timelines (pure, Node-testable) src/github.js REST client: repos, sampled stargazer pages src/charts.js D3: circle-pack map, birth-year columns, stacked sta
articles.summary: 开源工具 Repo-Atlas 可按 GitHub 用户名生成仓库主题聚类地图，标注各组亮点、星标趋势与过时收藏。

articles.title: SVAR Gantt v2.8 for React, Svelte, Vue: upgraded scheduling engine & live updates
articles.content: We’re excited to announce version 2.8 of the SVAR Gantt chart components for React , Vue , and Svelte . This release makes the scheduling engine more than a display layer: it now handles many of the scheduling scenarios project managers deal with in real projects. With this update, SVAR Gantt PRO becomes a stronger tool for project planning and resource allocation. In version 2.8, we introduce an upgraded scheduling engine that takes auto-scheduling in SVAR Gantt PRO to the next level: Auto-scheduling across all four dependency types: FS, SS, FF, and SF. Critical path and slack now calculated based on all dependency types. Six scheduling constraints set the boundaries a plan must respect. Resource-driven scheduling calculates task dates from the working calendars of assigned people. Faster scheduling for auto-scheduling and critical path, which now run much faster with thousands of tasks. To make SVAR Gantt a more complete tool for project management and resource planning, we also added: Extended resource planning with a resource histogram and drag-and-drop resource assignment. New project tracking features , such as the progress line and S-curve. Sub-grid panel for task details shown to the right of the Gantt chart. Real-time server updates that support multi-user editing and collaboration. 🔹 See full changelog : React Gantt • Vue Gantt • Svelte Gantt 🔹 View demos for v2.8 : React Gantt • Vue Gantt • Svelte Gantt The following sections cover what ships in SVAR Gantt PRO . The MIT edition also gains three features of its own, listed at the end. Upgraded Scheduling Engine We’ve upgraded the scheduling engine of SVAR Gantt PRO to provide automatic scheduling logic for project planning: All four link types in auto-scheduling and the critical path Auto-scheduling previously supported only Finish-to-Start links, but in 2.8 we added support for Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish, and Start-to-Finish links, with lag applied to every link type. All four link types now affect dates, slack, and the critical path , which means overlapping work can be planned as it happens in real projects. When a linked task changes, the engine always recalculates the dates of its dependent tasks. 👉 Auto-scheduling demo: React • Svelte • Vue Manual and inactive tasks For more flexibility, we also added two task modes that take tasks out of auto-scheduling: manual and inactive tasks. Manual tasks are locked in place: auto-scheduling never moves them, while users can still drag them manually. This separates committed work from work that is still being planned. Inactive tasks represent work that has been cancelled or put on hold. The inactiveTasks feature enables support for inactive tasks in the grid and editor; to make a specific task inactive, set its inactive field to true . Marking a task as inactive keeps it visible on the chart while removing it from scheduling, the critical path, resource load, and progress tracking. articles.title: kafka-harbor: the Kafka layer every Node.js team rebuilds by hand, done once
articles.content: I have written the same five hundred lines on top of a Kafka client more times than I want to admit. Different companies, different clients, same code: retry with a delay, a dead-letter topic, commit only after the handler succeeded, shut down without losing the message in flight. Every time it was "just a small wrapper", and every time it grew into the part of the service nobody wanted to touch. So I wrote it once, properly, and published it. kafka-harbor hit 1.0.0 this week. This post is about why it exists and what it does that the clients don't. The clients stop at the protocol Every Kafka client for Node.js gives you a producer, a consumer, and good luck. That is not a complaint; it is their job. @confluentinc/kafka-javascript , kafkajs , @platformatic/kafka : they all speak the wire protocol well, and they all stop there. Your service needs more than the protocol. It needs an answer to questions like: The handler threw. Now what? Retry? How many times? With what delay? Where does the message go when you give up? The process got a SIGTERM with a handler halfway through a database write. Does the offset get committed? Does the message get redelivered? Does anyone find out? The retry produce failed because the broker was away for a second. Did the offset get committed anyway, and the message vanish? If you are on the JVM, Spring Kafka answers all of that for you. On Node.js, you answer it yourself, in every project, slightly differently each time. What kafka-harbor is It is not a client. It runs on top of one, through a small ClientAdapter interface. Two adapters ship with it: one wraps Confluent's client (librdkafka underneath), the other wraps @platformatic/kafka , pure TypeScript, no native binding. The core never sees a client type, and the same contract test suite runs against both, so switching clients is a one-line change that does not touch a single handler. import { createHarbor } from ' kafka-harbor ' import { confluentAdapter } from ' kafka-harbor/adapters/confluent ' const harbor = createHarbor ({ clientId : ' orders-service ' , brokers : [ ' kafka-1:9092 ' , ' kafka-2:9092 ' ], adapter : confluentAdapter () }) const consumer = harbor . consumer ({ groupId : ' orders-workers ' , retry : { levels : [{ delay : ' 5s ' }, { delay : ' 1m ' }, { delay : ' 10m ' }] }, autoCreateTopics : true }) consumer . subscribe < Order > ( ' orders ' , async ( message , ctx ) => { await fulfill ( message . value ) ctx . logger . info ( `order ${ message . key } done on attempt ${ ctx . attempt } ` ) }) await consumer . start () harbor . enableSignalHandlers () Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode That is the whole setup. If fulfill throws, the message goes to orders-retry-1 , waits five seconds, runs again. Fails again: orders-retry-2 , one minute. Then ten. Then orders-dlq . On SIGTERM, running handlers finish, their offsets commit, the consumer leaves the group, the client disconnects. The design principle behind every decision in the library:
articles.summary: 开源项目 kafka-harbor 封装 Node.js 团队反复手写的 Kafka 重试、死信队列、提交与优雅关闭逻辑。

articles.title: Croft: Typed data pipeline – in TypeScript and DuckDB
articles.content: # croft > croft is one command-line tool for local data pipelines in TypeScript, on one DuckDB file: it ingests APIs and files, transforms them with SQL or TypeScript, keeps the tables fresh on a schedule, and lets an app read them. It needs only Bun, and it is built to be driven by a coding agent. These docs describe croft 0.3.0, the version on npm as @zabaca/croft. Every link is a Markdown page; https://croft.zabaca.com/llms-full.txt is all of them in one file. Inside a croft project, `croft docs ` prints the same Guides, Reference and error pages offline, for the version that project pins. Install: `bun add -g @zabaca/croft`, then `croft init my-data`. croft needs Bun 1.3.14 or newer on macOS or Linux. ## Start here - [What croft is](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs.md): croft is one command-line tool for local data pipelines in TypeScript, on one DuckDB file, built to be driven by an agent. - [Install](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/install.md): croft needs Bun 1.3.14 or newer on macOS or Linux. One global launcher, and a pinned copy per project. - [Quickstart](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/quickstart.md): A croft project, a SQL transform, an API ingest and a schedule, in about five minutes. Every output on this page is from a real run of croft 0.1.0. - [With Claude Code and other agents](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/agents.md): What croft gives an agent, where an agent finds the docs, and the one permission rule that keeps every destructive step with the person. ## Concepts - [The seven concepts](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/concepts.md): Asset, run, key, incremental, check, schedule and secret. Everything else croft either infers or brings up when it is needed. - [Runs, staleness and previews](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/runs.md): How croft decides what to run, what a run does when one asset fails, and the three ways to try a change, from cheapest to most real. - [Safety: confirm, trash, restore](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/safety.md): Nothing implicit destroys ingested data. What needs a confirmation, what goes to the trash, and how to bring it back. ## Guides - [Writing an ingest: API and file templates](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/guides/ingest.md): croft docs ingest: API and file templates - [Writing an SQL asset: the header, one SELECT, and how it is rebuilt](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/guides/sql.md): croft docs sql: the header, one SELECT, and how it is rebuilt - [Writing a TypeScript transform: per-row (API or LLM) and whole-table templates](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/guides/transforms.md): croft docs transforms: per-row (API or LLM) and whole-table templates - [Checks: rules every write must pass, the same in TypeScript and SQL](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/guides/checks.md): croft docs checks: rules every write must pass, the same in TypeScript and SQL - [Scheduling: ingests that run on their own, and transforms that follow them](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/guides/scheduling.md): croft docs scheduling: ingests that run
